notes.subtopic: 1. Big Picture — End of the Medieval Period
notes.content:
**Executive summary:** The medieval period in India drew to a close after **Aurangzeb's death (1707)**. The Mughal Empire shrank to the area **around Delhi**; the British called the emperor the **'King of Delhi'** instead of 'Emperor of India'. The **Revolt of 1857** finally ended the dynasty. Most historians take the **mid-18th century** as the start of the **Modern Period** in India.

As the Mughals declined, foreign companies — **English (EEIC), French, Dutch, Portuguese** — grew powerful, and **regional kingdoms** arose.

**Chapter map:** Causes of decline (7) → Later Mughals → Foreign invasions → Regional kingdoms (Marathas, Hyderabad, Bengal, Mysore, Awadh, Rajputs, Sikhs).

fiveW.what: Intolerant religious policy and endless Deccan wars
fiveW.why: Religious rigidity; ambition to crush the Marathas
fiveW.how: Re-imposed jizyah and pilgrimage tax; spent 25 years fighting in the Deccan

notes.content:
• Did not realise **religious tolerance** was essential for a vast, diverse empire.
• **Re-imposed jizyah** and the **pilgrimage tax** on non-Muslims → alienated them.
• Akbar had won over the **Rajputs**; under Aurangzeb the **Rajputs, Sikhs, Jats and Satnamis revolted**.
• Spent the **last 25 years** trying to subdue the **Marathas in the Deccan** → **drain on the treasury**; the North became a centre of revolt; nobles declared independence; **administration broke down**.

**But — Aurangzeb is not solely responsible:** the empire survived **~150 years** after his death; other causes also contributed.

notes.subtopic: 3. Causes — Weak Successors, Succession Wars, Court Politics
notes.content:
**Weak successors (Later Mughals):** pleasure-loving, weak, incompetent → nobles grew powerful and manipulated rulers; distant **governors declared independence**.

| Later Mughals | Reign |
|---|---|
| Bahadur Shah I | 1707–12 |
| Jahandar Shah | 1712–13 |
| Farrukhsiyar | 1713–19 |
| **Muhammad Shah** | 1719–48 (Nadir Shah's invasion) |
| Ahmad Shah Bahadur | 1748–54 |
| Alamgir II | 1754–59 |
| **Shah Alam II** | 1759–1806 |
| Akbar II | 1806–37 |
| **Bahadur Shah Zafar** (last) | 1837–58 |

**Wars of succession:** no clear rule of succession → relatives fought → resources drained.

**Court politics — four groups of nobles:** **Iranis** (Persia), **Turanis** (Transoxiana), **Afghans** (across the Indus), **Hindustanis** — constant power struggle collapsed the administration.

fiveW.what: Foreign invasions that exposed Mughal weakness
fiveW.how: Nadir Shah looted and plundered Delhi in Muhammad Shah's reign

notes.content:
• **Failure of the mansabdari system** (introduced by **Akbar**): too many mansabdars, too few jagirs → conflict; mansabdars **did not keep the required troops** → weak army.
• **Jagirdari crisis:** scramble for better jagirs; emperors gave away **crown lands** → **loss of revenue** → decline of the emperor's power.
• **No military reform:** old equipment and techniques; **no navy** (Europeans had strong navies).
• **Foreign invasions:** **Nadir Shah** (Iran) — **1739**, looted **Delhi** (reign of Muhammad Shah; took the **Koh-i-Noor**); **Ahmad Shah Abdali** (Afghanistan) — **1761**.
• **End:** Bahadur Shah Zafar, leader of the **Revolt of 1857**, was **deported to Burma** → end of the Mughal Empire.

**Now:** the Koh-i-Noor is set in the British crown (Queen Alexandra's crown).

fiveW.who: Peshwas Balaji Vishwanath, Baji Rao I, Balaji Baji Rao; Maratha chiefs
fiveW.where: Deccan → Malwa, Gujarat, Bihar, Orissa, Delhi, Punjab
fiveW.what: Rise of a pan-Indian Maratha power and the Maratha Confederacy
fiveW.why: To fill the vacuum left by the Mughal decline
fiveW.how: Collected chauth and sardeshmukhi; divided conquered provinces among chiefs

notes.content:
**Peshwa** = Prime Minister who actually controlled the Maratha kingdom, while the king was a figurehead.

• **Balaji Vishwanath (1713–20):** strengthened **Shahu**; won from the Mughals (1719) the **right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi** in the Deccan; made the Peshwa the real power.
• **Baji Rao I (1720–40):** policy of **northward expansion** — Malwa, Gujarat, Bundelkhand; reached Delhi.
• **Balaji Baji Rao (1740–61):** shifted capital from **Satara to Poona**; Marathas reached **Bihar and Orissa** (east) and **Delhi and Punjab** (north) — **peak** of Maratha power.

**Maratha Confederacy:** chiefs ruled their own regions — **Sindhias** (Gwalior), **Holkars** (Indore), **Gaekwads** (Baroda), **Bhonsles** (Nagpur); the **Peshwa** was the official head.

**Taxes:** **Chauth** = one-fourth of revenue; **Sardeshmukhi** = an additional one-tenth.

fiveW.why: Maratha conquest of Punjab clashed with Abdali
fiveW.how: Marathas had no allies and knew guerrilla, not open, warfare

notes.content:
• The Maratha conquest of **Punjab** brought them into conflict with **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.
• The Marathas, **with no allies**, were **completely routed** in **1761**.
• Used to **guerrilla warfare**, they did not know much about **open warfare**.
• **Results:** ended Maratha ambition of controlling the Mughal Empire; the Afghans also failed to replace the Mughals → **paved the way for the EEIC**.

**Three battles of Panipat**
| Battle | Year | Result |
|---|---|---|
| First | 1526 | **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** → Mughal Empire founded |
| Second | 1556 | **Akbar** defeated **Hemu** |
| Third | 1761 | **Abdali** defeated the **Marathas** |

**Hyderabad**
• Founded in **1724** by **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah**, Mughal viceroy of the Deccan.
• Never officially declared independence but was **in reality independent**; successors = **Nizams of Hyderabad**.
• Set up an **efficient administration**; protected the state internally and externally.

**Bengal**
• **Murshid Quli Khan**, the Mughal governor, made Bengal virtually independent (capital **Murshidabad**).
• **Alivardi Khan** encouraged **Indian and foreign merchants** to trade in Bengal.
• His grandson **Siraj-ud-Daulah** — **last independent Nawab of Bengal**; betrayed by his men and defeated by the British at **Plassey (1757)**.

fiveW.who: Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan (Mysore); Saadat Khan, Safdar Jang, Shuja-ud-Daulah (Awadh)
fiveW.why: Able rulers used the Mughal decline to build independent states
fiveW.how: Army and revenue reforms; encouraged trade, industry and culture

notes.content:
**Mysore**
• **Hyder Ali** rose from a **soldier to commander**; became ruler in **1761**; made Mysore powerful and prosperous — alarmed the **Nizam, Marathas and British**.
• **Tipu Sultan** (his son): reformed and strengthened the army; encouraged **trade, industry, agriculture**; fought the **Anglo-Mysore Wars**; **died a hero's death defending his capital** (Srirangapatnam, 1799).

**Awadh (Oudh)**
• Founded by **Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan** (Mughal governor) → **Safdar Jang** → his son **Shuja-ud-Daulah**.
• Saadat Khan reformed **revenue collection** and strengthened the army → peace and prosperity.
• Capital **Lucknow** → distinct **Lucknawi culture** in literature, art, architecture.
• **Safdar Jang's tomb** (Delhi) shows the Nawabs' prestige.

fiveW.who: Ranjit Singh and the Sikh misls; Rajput states
fiveW.when: 18th century; Treaty of Amritsar 1809; Ranjit Singh died 1839
fiveW.where: Punjab and Jammu; Jaipur, Mewar, Marwar
fiveW.what: Sikh kingdom from the Khyber Pass to Sindh
fiveW.why: Mughal hold on Punjab weakened after Nadir Shah and Abdali
fiveW.how: Ranjit Singh united twelve misls; treaty with the British fixed the Sutlej boundary

notes.content:
**Rajputs:** **Jaipur, Mewar, Marwar** asserted independence but **never united**; internal strife made them prey to British expansion.
• **Sawai Jai Singh** of Amber (Jaipur, ruler from **1699**) — wise ruler; discouraged **sati**; built the **Jantar Mantar** observatories.

**Sikhs**
• Took control of **Punjab and Jammu**; organised into **12 misls** (groups).
• **Ranjit Singh** united them and became master of Punjab.
• **Treaty of Amritsar (1809)** — 'treaty of **perpetual friendship**'; **Sutlej River** = boundary between British and Sikh lands.
• At his death (**1839**) his kingdom stretched from the **Khyber Pass to Sindh**; afterwards Punjab was **annexed** by the British.

questions.question: Why can Aurangzeb not be held solely responsible for the decline of the Mughal Empire?
questions.answer:
• The Mughal Empire continued for about 150 years after his death.
  • His weak, pleasure-loving successors lost control over nobles and governors.
  • Wars of succession, court factions, failure of the mansabdari and jagirdari systems, and no military reform also weakened it.
  • Foreign invasions (Nadir Shah 1739, Abdali 1761) and the rise of regional powers hastened the decline.
questions.topperTip: Start with the '150 years' fact — it is the single strongest argument.

questions.question: Was Aurangzeb's failure to realise the need for religious tolerance a cause of the decline? Give reasons.
questions.answer:
Yes.

  • A vast and diverse empire needed tolerance, as Akbar had shown by winning over the Rajputs.
  • Aurangzeb re-imposed the jizyah and pilgrimage tax, alienating non-Muslims.
  • This led to revolts of the Rajputs, Sikhs, Jats and Satnamis, and long wars with the Marathas that emptied the treasury.

questions.question: Into how many groups were the nobles in the Mughal court divided? Name them.
questions.answer:
Four groups:

  • Iranis — from Persia
  • Turanis — from Transoxiana (Central Asia)
  • Afghans — from the mountainous regions across the Indus
  • Hindustanis — Indian-born nobles

Their constant power struggle collapsed the administration.

questions.question: Explain the failure of the mansabdari system and the jagirdari crisis.
questions.answer:
• Mansabdari: introduced by Akbar and efficient under him; later the number of mansabdars grew but jagirs did not → conflict; mansabdars did not maintain required troops → weak army.
  • Jagirdari crisis: scramble for better jagirs; weak emperors controlled by nobles gave away crown lands → loss of revenue for the treasury → emperor's power declined.

questions.question: What was the effect of the invasions of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali?
questions.answer:
• Nadir Shah (Iran) invaded in 1739 during Muhammad Shah's reign, looted and plundered Delhi (carried off the Koh-i-Noor).
  • Ahmad Shah Abdali (Afghanistan) invaded repeatedly; defeated the Marathas at Panipat (1761).
  • They exposed the weak defence of the empire, drained its wealth and weakened Mughal hold over Punjab.

questions.question: How did the Marathas establish a pan-Indian empire? Discuss two achievements of Balaji Vishwanath.
questions.answer:
• Balaji Vishwanath: (i) strengthened Shahu's rule and made the Peshwa the real power; (ii) secured from the Mughals the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi in the Deccan (1719).
  • Baji Rao I: expanded north into Malwa, Gujarat, Bundelkhand.
  • Balaji Baji Rao: moved capital to Poona; Marathas reached Bihar, Orissa, Delhi and Punjab.
  • Conquered provinces were divided among the chiefs of the Maratha Confederacy (Sindhias, Holkars, Gaekwads, Bhonsles).

questions.question: Why did the Marathas fail to gain control over the Mughal Empire? How did this help the EEIC?
questions.answer:
• Their conquest of Punjab brought them into conflict with Ahmad Shah Abdali.
  • At the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) they had no allies and, used to guerrilla warfare, lacked skill in open warfare — they were routed.
  • The Afghans too failed to replace the Mughals.
  • This left a power vacuum that the EEIC filled through wars and diplomacy.
questions.topperTip: End with the 'power vacuum → EEIC' line — it links this chapter to Ch 5–7.

questions.question: Describe the rule of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah. What were his successors called?
questions.answer: Mughal viceroy of the Deccan who founded Hyderabad in 1724. He never officially declared independence but ruled as an independent ruler. He set up an efficient administration and protected the state internally and externally. His successors were called the Nizams of Hyderabad.

questions.question: Who was Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan? Who succeeded him?
questions.answer: A Mughal governor who founded the independent state of Awadh. An efficient administrator, he reformed revenue collection and strengthened the army. He was succeeded by Safdar Jang, and then by Safdar Jang's son Shuja-ud-Daulah.

questions.question: (Picture) Identify the Mysore ruler who died defending his capital. Name his father.
(Picture) Grandson of the founder of Awadh: name him, his father and his capital.
'Internal strife led to the annexation of the Rajput kingdoms by the British.' Do you support the statement?
questions.answer: Yes. Jaipur, Mewar and Marwar asserted independence after the Mughal decline, but they never put up a united front and followed separate policies. Their internal conflicts weakened them, and the former pillars of the Mughal Empire became prey to British expansionist policies.

questions.question: Describe the rise of the Sikh kingdom under Ranjit Singh.
questions.answer:
• After Nadir Shah and Abdali, the Mughal hold on Punjab weakened; the Sikhs took Punjab and Jammu and formed 12 misls.
  • Ranjit Singh united them and became master of Punjab.
  • Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with the British — Sutlej as boundary ('perpetual friendship').
  • At his death (1839), his kingdom stretched from the Khyber Pass to Sindh; later annexed by the British.
